fix(mysql): indent procedural bodies, conditions and assignment lists
### Brief summary of the change made

**Size note** - this is only +55/-49 of grammar (and even that's the same moves repeated over similar constructs) with minor fixture changes which look big due to indent level making a line appear to change, and some tests.

Follow-up to #8531, where @keraion asked for `Indent`/`Dedent` in the
`BEGIN ... END` body.  The other bodies and lists had the same indent gap, and I also [said in #8531](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/pull/8531#discussion_r4057742788) that I would unify some similar constructs (which makes sense as the MySQL/MariaDB parser source does too).  After looking at the recent `IF` improvements (#8380), it makes sense to do it as a segment (`statement_list`) rather than a grammar because `IF` already needs a node per branch to mark where each branch ends.  

As such, this fixes them all together, following one rule:

- **A nested statement is indented under its header.** A `BEGIN ... END`
  block keeps `BEGIN` and `END` at the header's level and indents its own
  contents; a body written as a single statement is indented under the header.
- **A statement's own list of assignments or actions is indented,** as
  `UPDATE ... SET` already is.
- **A condition that runs onto more lines is indented,** as a `WHERE`
  clause's is.
- **A query that is a statement's payload stays flat,** as `INSERT ... SELECT`
  and `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` already do. `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT` is
  unchanged.

Changes, all in `dialect_mysql.py` (MariaDB inherits them):

- `BEGIN ... END`, `WHILE`, `LOOP` and `REPEAT` bodies are indented. For
  `REPEAT`, `UNTIL` lines up with `REPEAT`.
- `IF`, `ELSEIF`, `WHILE` and `UNTIL` conditions take an implicit indent, as
  `WHERE` and `CASE WHEN` do. Until now a multi-line condition was flattened
  to the keyword's level. By default `fix` now puts a line break after the
  keyword; with `implici

DuckDB: Parse expressions in SET VARIABLE assignments
### Brief summary of the change made

DuckDB supports expressions and scalar subqueries in `SET VARIABLE`, but SQLFluff rejects assignments such as:

```sql
SET VARIABLE total = 1 + 2;
SET VARIABLE answer = (SELECT 42);
```

Use `ExpressionSegment` for the assigned value. Add fixtures for arithmetic, a function call, scalar and aggregate subqueries, and existing list/date literal assignments. Both `=` and `TO` are covered.

Reference: [DuckDB SET VARIABLE documentation](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/sql/statements/set_variable).

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

Only the SET VARIABLE value grammar changes; configuration-setting grammar is unchanged. Existing variable literal values gain an `expression` wrapper in the parse tree, reflected in the generated fixture.

- DuckDB dialect tests: 123 passed.

- `pre-commit run --all-files` passed, including mypy, Ruff, YAML linting, and codespell.
- Executed all six added assignments on DuckDB 1.5.6 and checked each stored value with `getvariable()`.
- Regenerated all 2,312 parser fixtures; no unrelated fixture changes.
- Regenerated Rust grammar; `utils/rustify.py check` passed.

fix(mysql): parse BEGIN...END bodies as compound statements
### Brief summary of the change made

Makes progress on #901, and related to #3599.

Every MySQL/MariaDB routine body with more than one statement is currently
mis-parsed, silently: `BEGIN` is read as a transaction start and the remaining
statements escape to file scope, so rules run against a tree that doesn't
represent the SQL. Three existing fixtures encode that wrong tree, so CI enforces
the bug on every run. They are corrected here.

**Size, for triage:** the grammar change is 83 lines added and 63 removed, all in
`dialect_mysql.py`. The other 98 files are 12 new fixtures (`.sql` and `.yml`
each) and 74 regenerated `.yml` trees; most of the regenerated trees differ only
because bodies now nest inside `compound_statement`.

MySQL compound statement bodies were not contained in the parse tree.
`FunctionDefinitionGrammar` matched `TransactionStatementSegment`, so `BEGIN`
was parsed as a transaction start and the statements that followed escaped to
file scope rather than nesting inside the routine. No error was raised, so
rules ran against a tree that did not represent the SQL.

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION f1(p1 INT) RETURNS INT DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN
    DECLARE v1 INT;
    SET v1 = p1 * 2;
    RETURN v1;
END
```

`create_function_statement` ended at the first internal `;`, and `SET` and
`RETURN` appeared as top level statements beside it.

The underlying cause is that `BEGIN` is two unrelated keywords in MySQL:
transaction control, closed by `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`, and a compound
statement, closed by `END`. Only the first was modelled, so blocks existed as a
side effect of transaction parsing rather than in their own right.

This adds `CompoundStatementSegment` — optional label, `BEGIN`, a delimited
statement list, `END`, optional end label, per
https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/begin-end.html — and uses it for
`CREATE PROCEDURE` and `CREATE FUNCTION` bodies, `CREAT

Databricks: restore LIVE and STREAMING LIVE view support
### Brief summary of the change made

The `databricks` dialect rejects three forms its own reference documents, all dropped when #7405 rewrote `CreateViewStatementSegment` from scratch instead of subclassing `sparksql`:

- Pipeline views: `CREATE [OR REPLACE] [GLOBAL] TEMPORARY [STREAMING] LIVE VIEW ...` — `sparksql` parses them, so the dialect named after Databricks was the one that could not.
- The temporary view backed by a data source: `CREATE [OR REPLACE] TEMPORARY VIEW name [column_list] USING data_source [OPTIONS (...)]`.
- The parenthesised `with_clause` list: `WITH ( schema_binding [, ...] )`.

`test/fixtures/dialects/sparksql/databricks_dlt_create_view.sql` has covered the pipeline forms since well before that change. It simply was never exercised under the `databricks` dialect, so nothing failed.

Restored here:

- `LIVE`, with `STREAMING` bound to it rather than independently optional, because there is no `CREATE STREAMING VIEW`.
- `OR REFRESH` is deliberately **not** accepted on a view. It belongs to streaming tables and materialized views, which have their own segments; the corpus of published Databricks SQL uses it with `MATERIALIZED VIEW`, `STREAMING TABLE` and `LIVE TABLE`, and with no `VIEW` form at all.
- The data-source production, whose `TEMPORARY` is unbracketed (so `CREATE VIEW v USING csv` stays rejected) and whose `USING` data source and `OPTIONS` name-value pairs are all required.
- The parenthesised `with_clause` list, as an alternative to the existing `WITH SCHEMA ...` and `WITH METRICS` forms.
- `ConstraintStatementSegment` in the column list, so pipeline expectations (`CONSTRAINT valid_a EXPECT (a IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`) parse.

The LIVE schema is [deprecated](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/live-schema) in favour of the default publishing mode, but the page is explicit that "you can still use legacy publishing mode and the LIVE virtual schema for pipelines tha

SparkSQL: support EXECUTE IMMEDIATE
### Brief summary of the change made

`EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` was not implemented in this dialect at all. Not just the
argument clauses — the simplest form was unparsable too:

```sql
EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT 1';
```

[Spark's reference](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-ref-syntax-aux-exec-imm.html)
gives:

```
EXECUTE IMMEDIATE sql_string
  [ INTO var_name [, ...] ]
  [ USING { arg_expr [ AS ] [ alias ] } [, ...] ]
```

and adds that "for compatibility with other SQL dialects, `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE`
also supports `USING ( { arg_expr [ AS ] [alias] } [, ...] )`".

[Databricks documents the same grammar](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-aux-execute-immediate),
down to that bracketed form, so this goes in SparkSQL and `databricks`
inherits it rather than being written twice.

Four details taken from the references and Spark's own parser rather than
guessed:

- **`sql_string` is an expression**, as in Spark's parser, so it is not
  limited to a literal or a variable. The reference's own last example needs
  that: `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'SELECT ' || func || '(c1) ...' USING 5 + 7 AS first`.
- **`INTO` takes multipart identifiers**, again following Spark's parser, so a
  session variable can be qualified: `INTO session.v1`,
  `INTO system.session.v1`.
- **`AS` is optional** before an alias. Spark's test suite uses the lower-case
  `as` spelling.
- **`INTO` takes no brackets.** See below.

Found in a published Databricks notebook on parameterised queries, and in
Spark's own `execute-immediate.sql` test input.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

`INTO (a, b)` is deliberately **not** accepted. Spark's test file labels that
line `-- INTO does not support braces - parser error`, and the syntax block
gives `INTO var_name [, ...]` unbracketed. The Databricks parameter
description writes the heading as `INTO ( var_name [, ...] )`, which looks
like a contradiction

SQLite: Parse multiple ON CONFLICT clauses in INSERT
### Brief summary of the change made

SQLite allows multiple `ON CONFLICT` clauses in one INSERT, but SQLFluff reports a parse error at the second clause. For example:

```sql
INSERT INTO t1 (a, b) VALUES (1, 2)
ON CONFLICT (a) DO UPDATE SET b = excluded.b
ON CONFLICT (b) DO NOTHING;
```

Allow repeated targeted UPSERT clauses after both VALUES and SELECT, followed by at most one final targetless clause. Add SQL/YAML fixtures covering multiple targets, a conditional update, a final targetless clause, and RETURNING.

Reference: [SQLite UPSERT documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_upsert.html). Multiple clauses have been supported since SQLite 3.35.0.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

This changes only SQLite INSERT parsing. Existing zero- and single-clause inserts remain covered by the dialect fixtures.

### Validation

- New fixture failed before the grammar change, at the second `ON CONFLICT`.
- SQLite dialect tests: 117 passed, including six invalid targetless-clause ordering cases.
- Full Python suite: 11,485 passed, 2,636 skipped (Python 3.12).
- `pre-commit run --all-files` passed, including mypy, Ruff, YAML linting, and codespell.
- Executed all three added statements against SQLite 3.53.4, checking resulting rows across 10 insertion/conflict scenarios.
- Regenerated all 2,312 parser fixtures; no unrelated fixture changes.
- Regenerated Rust dialect tables; `utils/rustify.py check` passed.

- [x] Linked the documented SQLite syntax.

Databricks: parse DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW
### Brief summary of the change made

`DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW` is unparsable in the `databricks` dialect. The
[reference](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-drop-view)
gives:

```
DROP [ MATERIALIZED ] VIEW [ IF EXISTS ] view_name
```

and its own example uses `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW employeeView`. The dialect
inherited the ANSI segment, which accepts only `DROP VIEW`, so the documented
materialized form fails:

```sql
DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW employeeview;   -- was unparsable
```

The fix inserts `MATERIALIZED` as an optional keyword ahead of `VIEW` in a
`databricks`-only override of `DropViewStatementSegment`. Apache Spark has no
materialized views, so `sparksql` is deliberately left alone.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

None beyond the widening: `DROP VIEW` and `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS` parse exactly
as before, and `DROP MATERIALIZED` with no view is still rejected. The fixture
covers the plain, `IF EXISTS` and schema-qualified forms, and `DROP VIEW`
remains covered by the existing sparksql fixture this dialect shares.

### What tests/validation did you carry out?

- `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW mv`, `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW IF EXISTS mv` and
  `DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW cat.sch.mv` parse; the `DROP VIEW` forms are
  unchanged.
- `DROP MATERIALIZED` (dangling, no view) is still rejected.
- Whole `test/dialects/` directory: **7021 passed**.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` clean on the changed file.

The syntax is taken from the reference page linked above, and the statement
was found against a corpus of published Databricks SQL.

SparkSQL/Databricks: accept NOT NULL and COLLATE on a struct field
### Brief summary of the change made

Databricks documents a `STRUCT` field as

```
STRUCT < [fieldName [:] fieldType [NOT NULL] [COLLATE collationName] [COMMENT str] [, …] ] >
```

([STRUCT type](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/data-types/struct-type))

`StructTypeSchemaSegment` had the identifier, the optional colon, the type
and the comment — but neither clause in between. So
`STRUCT<a: INT COMMENT 'c'>` parsed while `STRUCT<a: INT NOT NULL>` and
`STRUCT<a: STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE>` were unparsable, even though all
three sit in the same production.

**`NOT NULL` is Spark's, so it is fixed in `sparksql`.** Spark's grammar has
it:

```
complexColType
    : errorCapturingIdentifier COLON? dataType (errorCapturingNot NULL)? commentSpec?
    ;
```

`databricks` inherits this segment, so it is fixed there too.

**`COLLATE` is Databricks', so it activates only there** — without a second
copy of the segment. ANSI already defines `CollateGrammar` as `Nothing()`,
`sparksql` does not override it, and `dialect_databricks.py` already defines
it as `Sequence("COLLATE", Ref("CollationReferenceSegment"))`. Adding
`Ref("CollateGrammar", optional=True)` in the documented position is
therefore inert for `sparksql` and every other dialect inheriting the
segment, and live for `databricks` alone. Restating the whole segment in
`dialect_databricks.py` would have worked too, but a restated segment is how
this dialect lost `LIVE` views in #7405, so the extension point seemed the
safer shape.

`STRING COLLATE UTF8_LCASE` already parsed as a top-level column and inside
a `CAST`; it just could not be nested.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

Narrow by construction. `NOT` and `NULL` are bound together as one optional
`Sequence` rather than two independent optional keywords, and both clauses
are positionally bound rather than floating:

| statement | `spa

DuckDB: Parse human-readable ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES values
### Brief summary of the change made

```sql
COPY (SELECT 42 AS value) TO 'output.parquet' (
    FORMAT parquet,
    ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES '2MB'
);
```

Allow `QuotedLiteralSegment` alongside `NumericLiteralSegment` for this COPY TO option. Add SQL/YAML fixtures covering `'2MB'` and `2097152`.

Reference: [DuckDB Parquet COPY options](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/sql/statements/copy#parquet-options).

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

The grammar change is limited to this DuckDB option; numeric values remain supported.

perf(rust): cut frame-engine allocation and copying
<!--Thanks for adding this feature!-->

<!--Please give the Pull Request a meaningful title for the release notes-->

### Brief summary of the change made
<!--Please include `fixes #XXXX` to automatically close any corresponding issue when the pull request is merged. Alternatively if not fully closed you can say `makes progress on #XXXX`.-->
This removes a good number of the allocations and copies that happen within the frame engine

- Share terminator sets as `Arc<[GrammarId]>`: ~40% of frames spilled the `SmallVec<4>`, ~17% of parse allocations.
- `Box` compound `FrameContext` states: `TableParseFrame` 312B -> 144B, `memmove` 17% -> 5% of samples.
- `settle_frame`: combine/commit `Combining` and `Complete` frames directly instead of a push/pop round trip.
- Share empty `MatchResult`s, pool frame-stack buffers, and read terminator/children ids straight from the grammar tables. (I have a follow up to get this a bit faster without needing `unsafe`)
- `check_and_handle_table_frame_cache` returns a `CacheLookup` enum.
- Remove the never-set `element_key` from the result hand-off.

Parse time -27% to -37% across dialects (-34.6% overall).

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?
None

### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #8646.

LT09's search for a comment between `SELECT` and the first newline stopped at a `select_clause_modifier`. This missed a trailing comment after `DISTINCT`, `ALL`, or `TOP`, allowing the autofix to move the select target into a line comment.

### Brief summary of the change made

makes progress on #8616

LT05 moves a long trailing comment before or after its line. When the source of the comment contains a Jinja tag, both moves corrupt the file:

- With `trailing_comments = before` (the default), LT05 builds the moved comment from the rendered text, so the tags are lost. The delete of the original is split at the tag placeholders, and `generate_source_patches` skips the parts that contain a tag.

Oracle: parse common SQL*Plus SET commands
### Brief summary of the change made

`SqlplusSetStatementSegment` only handled `SET SCAN ON|OFF`, so other SQL*Plus `SET` commands were unparsable. `SET DEFINE OFF` is really common at the top of Oracle scripts - it turns off substitution variables, so an `&` in a string literal is left alone - and because the unparsable section runs to the end of the file, a script like this didn't get linted at all:

```sql
SET DEFINE OFF
INSERT INTO tools (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Hammer & Tongs');
```

This adds the `SET` system variables that come up most in deployment scripts: `DEFINE`, `ECHO`, `ESCAPE`, `FEEDBACK`, `FLAGGER`, `HEADING`, `LINESIZE`, `LONG`, `NULL`, `PAGESIZE`, `SERVEROUTPUT`, `SQLBLANKLINES`, `SUFFIX`, `TERMOUT`, `TIME`, `TIMING`, `TRIMSPOOL` and `VERIFY`, alongside the existing `SCAN`. Syntax is from the [SET System Variable Summary](https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/26/sqpug/SET-system-variable-summary.html).

Names and values are plain keywords, with the new ones added to the Oracle unreserved keywords. Each variable takes its full name or its shortest documented abbreviation (e.g. `SERVEROUT`), one `SET` can set several of them (e.g. `SET ECHO OFF FEEDBACK OFF` - SQL*Plus accepts this even though the syntax summary shows one at a time), and it's still only tried at batch level. Each variable also only accepts its documented values rather than any tokens - SQL*Plus commands don't need a semicolon, so a looser grammar would end up swallowing the next line.

Unquoted text values for `NULL` and `SUFFIX` are plain text tokens rather than identifiers, so reserved words work (`SET NULL NULL`) and capitalisation rules leave the text alone. Double-quoted text is a literal rather than a quoted identifier, so RF05 doesn't flag it.

I've kept it to these variables so it's easy to review - happy to follow up with the rest of the list in another PR.

Postgres: accept PG 16-17 utility options and ON/OFF/0/1 option values
### Brief summary of the change made

fixes #8602

The postgres dialect reads a boolean option value with `BooleanLiteralGrammar`, which is only `TRUE` or `FALSE`. This change adds `OptionBooleanGrammar`, which also accepts `ON`, `OFF` and an unsigned number. It uses the new grammar in `EXPLAIN`, `ANALYZE`, `REINDEX` and `COPY`. It also uses the new grammar for `ALLOW_CONNECTIONS` and `IS_TEMPLATE` in `CREATE DATABASE` and `ALTER DATABASE`, and for `DETERMINISTIC` in `CREATE COLLATION`.

PostgreSQL reads these values with `utility_option_arg`, `copy_generic_opt_arg` and `createdb_opt_item` in `gram.y`. `CREATE COLLATION` reads the value as a `def_arg` in `gram.y`, and `DefineCollation` converts it with `defGetBoolean`. The new grammar accepts the six values that the `EXPLAIN` page lists (`TRUE`, `ON`, `1`, `FALSE`, `OFF`, `0`) and any unsigned number. `VACUUM` keeps its own value grammar, which reads `on` as an identifier.

The change also adds the options from PostgreSQL 16 and 17:

- `EXPLAIN`: `GENERIC_PLAN [ boolean ]`, `SERIALIZE [ NONE | TEXT | BINARY ]` and `MEMORY [ boolean ]`.
- `VACUUM`: `PROCESS_MAIN`, `SKIP_DATABASE_STATS`, `ONLY_DATABASE_STATS` and `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT`.
- `ANALYZE`: `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT`, with a number or a quoted size such as `'1MB'`.

The 7 new option names go into `postgres_nondocs_keywords` as non-reserved keywords: `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT`, `GENERIC_PLAN`, `MEMORY`, `ONLY_DATABASE_STATS`, `PROCESS_MAIN`, `SERIALIZE` and `SKIP_DATABASE_STATS`. They stay unreserved, so a column or a table with one of these names still parses. New fixture statements in `explain.sql` and `vacuum.sql` use them as column names.

fix(CV07): guard one-sided liftable-whitespace fix independently
### Brief summary of the change made

Rule `CV07` (`convention.statement_brackets`, aliased `L053`) crashes with an
unhandled `AssertionError` on ordinary, valid SQL whenever a bracket-wrapped
top-level statement has liftable content (whitespace or an inline comment) on
only *one* side of its inner content — e.g.:

```sql
( SELECT foo FROM bar)
```

`CV07._eval` computes `leading`/`trailing` (liftable segments at the
start/end) separately, but gates `LintFix.create_before`/`create_after` on
their *combination* (`lift_nodes = leading + trailing`). Both calls assert a
non-empty edit list (`src/sqlfluff/core/rules/fix.py:78-80`), so whenever
exactly one side is empty — the common case, since most bracketed statements
don't have matching whitespace/comment on both sides — the empty side still
gets called and raises `AssertionError: A create fix must have an edit.`

Entry point: any `sqlfluff lint`/`sqlfluff fix` (CLI or the public API) with
`CV07`/`L053` enabled (default rule set) over such a file. Before the fix,
linting the example above raises the `AssertionError` with a full traceback,
and `sqlfluff fix` silently drops the fix instead of correcting the file.

A second bug in the same block: when `trailing` is empty,
`filtered_children[len(leading) : -len(trailing)]` evaluates `-len(trailing)`
as `-0 == 0`, truncating to an empty slice whenever `leading` is non-empty —
so patching only the assertion would make `fix()` silently drop the
statement's real content instead of crashing.

Fix: guard `create_before`/`create_after` independently on whether that
side's list is non-empty, and compute the trailing slice bound as
`len(filtered_children) - len(trailing)` so it degrades correctly to "keep
everything" when `trailing` is empty.
